reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: The commonest soft tissue tumour, composed of mature white adipocytes, typically presenting as a soft, mobile, painless subcutaneous mass
Most are superficial and small; deep-seated, intramuscular, or large lesions (over roughly ten centimetres) warrant greater suspicion for an atypical lipomatous tumour
On MRI a simple lipoma follows subcutaneous fat on all sequences and suppresses completely on fat-saturated images, with no thick septa or non-fatty nodules
Common cytogenetic events involve rearrangements of the 12q13-15 region affecting HMGA2, distinct from the MDM2 and CDK4 amplification seen in atypical lipomatous tumour
Multiple lipomas suggest familial multiple lipomatosis or syndromic associations such as Gardner syndrome, Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome, or benign symmetric lipomatosis (Madelung disease)
Variants include angiolipoma, spindle cell lipoma, and chondroid lipoma, each with characteristic histology
Asymptomatic superficial lipomas need no intervention; marginal excision is reserved for symptomatic, enlarging, or cosmetically troublesome lesions
Any deep or rapidly growing fatty mass should be imaged and, if atypical, biopsied before excision rather than simply shelled out
reference.pathophysiology: A lipoma is a benign clonal neoplasm of mature adipocytes rather than a simple overgrowth of normal fat. The majority are solitary, well-circumscribed, and enclosed by a thin fibrous capsule, arising most often in the subcutaneous tissue of the trunk, neck, and proximal limbs. A large proportion harbour clonal chromosomal rearrangements, most frequently involving the high-mobility group gene HMGA2 at 12q13-15, which drives adipocyte proliferation while preserving terminal differentiation, so the cells remain cytologically bland. The key biological distinction is from atypical lipomatous tumour and well-differentiated liposarcoma, which show amplification of MDM2 and CDK4 on 12q and carry a risk of dedifferentiation and local recurrence; this molecular separation, rather than morphology alone, underpins modern classification and management.
additionalDifferentials: Atypical lipomatous tumour and well-differentiated liposarcoma
Nodular fasciitis or other benign soft tissue proliferation
Myxoid soft tissue tumour when myxoid change is present
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound as a first-line assessment of a superficial soft tissue lump
MRI with fat-saturated sequences to confirm uncomplicated fat and exclude worrying features
Image-guided core biopsy for deep, large, or radiologically atypical lesions
MDM2 amplification testing by FISH when atypical lipomatous tumour is a consideration
Cross-sectional imaging of the affected compartment to define depth and relationship to muscle
Histological examination of the excised specimen to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Rapid growth, size beyond roughly ten centimetres, or a deep or intramuscular location
Pain, fixation to deeper structures, or overlying skin change
Thick or nodular septa, non-fatty enhancing components, or incomplete fat suppression on MRI
New neurological or vascular symptoms from local mass effect
reference.prognosis: Simple lipomas are benign with an excellent prognosis and rarely recur after complete marginal excision. The principal clinical task is to identify the minority of fatty masses that are in fact atypical lipomatous tumours, since these carry a risk of local recurrence and, in certain sites, dedifferentiation.
pitfalls: Assuming any fatty lump is a simple lipoma and shelling out a deep mass that proves to be an atypical lipomatous tumour
Failing to image deep or large lesions before intervention
Overlooking multiple lipomas as a clue to an underlying syndrome
Mistaking myxoid or spindle cell change for malignancy, or vice versa, without molecular confirmation
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
Bone and Soft Tissue Sarcoma clinical practice guidelines
management: Reassure and observe typical small, superficial, asymptomatic subcutaneous lipomas, which are benign and need no intervention
Offer marginal surgical excision for lesions that are symptomatic, enlarging, cosmetically troublesome or diagnostically uncertain

Characterise deep, large or radiologically atypical lesions with MRI using fat-saturated sequences, and obtain image-guided core biopsy with MDM2 amplification testing by FISH to exclude an atypical lipomatous tumour or well-differentiated liposarcoma
Refer to a specialist sarcoma service for wider excision when an atypical lipomatous tumour or liposarcoma is confirmed
Investigate for syndromic or familial multiple lipomatosis, such as Gardner syndrome, Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome or Madelung disease, when lipomas are multiple
Confirm the diagnosis histologically on the excised specimen
